title: Infectious Diseases and Hyperplasia of the Prostate
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the two common benign disorders of the prostate: benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and prostatitis. It explains why BPH depends on dihydrotestosterone, why it grows in the zone that wraps the urethra, and how outlet obstruction works its way back through the bladder, ureters, and kidneys. It then sorts prostatitis into acute bacterial, chronic bacterial, and chronic nonbacterial forms by organism, route, and time course. Board questions typically give an older man with urinary symptoms or a febrile man with a tender prostate and ask for the zone, the hormone, the organism, the complication, or the category.
prerequisites: Zonal anatomy of the prostate and the course of the prostatic urethra
Androgen synthesis and action, including 5-alpha-reductase and the androgen receptor (RE-1 to RE-4)
Micturition reflex and autonomic control of the detrusor and bladder neck
Glomerular filtration and the Starling forces across the glomerulus
Gram-negative rods, Neisseria, and Chlamydia: structure and virulence factors

connections.to: Renal physiology and acute kidney injury
connections.how: Back pressure from outlet obstruction raises Bowman's space pressure, lowers GFR, and produces postrenal kidney injury.

connections.to: Urinary tract infection and E. coli virulence
connections.how: The same uropathogenic gram-negative rods that cause cystitis reach the prostate by reflux of infected urine into the prostatic ducts.

BPH is hormone-driven hyperplasia, and detrusor thickening is hypertrophy in response to pressure overload.

sections.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia: DHT-driven nodular growth in the transition zone

blocks.text: The prostate is divided into zones with different diseases. The peripheral zone, posterior and next to the rectum, holds most of the glandular tissue. The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts. The transition zone is a small region on either side of the proximal prostatic urethra, together with the periurethral glands. BPH begins in the transition zone and periurethral tissue, which is why it narrows the urethra early, while carcinoma arises mostly in the peripheral zone, where it is palpable on rectal examination but slow to cause urinary symptoms.

BPH is hyperplasia: an increase in the number of cells, both epithelial and stromal, not an increase in cell size and not a neoplasm. It is extremely common, beginning in some men in their 40s and present histologically in most men by their 80s. Two conditions are required: age and functioning testes producing androgen. Men castrated before puberty and men with inherited 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency do not develop BPH.

blocks.title: How androgen drives BPH
steps: Testes secrete testosterone into the blood
Stromal 5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to DHT
DHT binds the androgen receptor in stromal and epithelial nuclei
Stromal cells release growth factors (FGF family members)
Epithelial and stromal proliferation rises; apoptosis falls
Nodules form in the transition zone and compress the urethra
blocks.caption: DHT acts mainly through stromal cells, which signal to neighboring epithelium in a paracrine fashion. The net gain in cells comes from both more proliferation and less programmed cell death.

blocks.text: DHT matters more than testosterone because it binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity and dissociates more slowly, giving a stronger, longer signal. Circulating testosterone falls modestly with age while BPH rises, so other factors contribute; a rising estrogen to testosterone ratio is thought to sensitize prostatic cells to DHT, but this role is less certain.

Grossly, the gland is firm to rubbery with well-defined nodules, some containing cysts of milky fluid. Microscopically, nodules of proliferating glands with papillary infoldings sit in hyperplastic fibromuscular stroma, and the glands keep two cell layers: inner columnar secretory cells and an outer flattened basal cell layer. Corpora amylacea (laminated concretions of secretion) are common. On rectal examination the gland is symmetrically enlarged, smooth, and rubbery, and the median sulcus may be lost.

blocks.title: BPH compared with prostate carcinoma
rows: Two cell layers; basal layer present
Common, because the urethra is compressed
Uncommon, because growth is away from the urethra
Often raised; can be normal early
blocks.caption: Both diseases are androgen dependent and common in older men, so they often coexist, but one does not turn into the other.

blocks.text: BPH is not a precursor of carcinoma. The two arise in different zones from different processes, and hyperplastic nodules do not progress through dysplasia to cancer. PSA, a serine protease made by prostatic epithelium, can rise mildly in BPH simply because there is more epithelium, so a raised PSA does not by itself distinguish the two.

blocks.predict: A 70-year-old man has a hard, irregular nodule on the posterior surface of his prostate but no urinary symptoms. Is this more likely BPH or carcinoma, and why?
blocks.explain: Carcinoma. The posterior gland felt on rectal examination is the peripheral zone, where most carcinomas arise; growth there is away from the urethra, so symptoms appear late. BPH arises around the urethra and gives smooth, rubbery enlargement with early symptoms.

sections.title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia: urinary findings and complications

blocks.text: BPH obstructs the bladder outlet in two ways. The static component is the mass of nodules compressing the prostatic urethra; nodules in the median lobe can also project into the bladder neck and act like a ball valve. The dynamic component is tone in prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle, which contracts through sympathetic alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Gland size correlates poorly with symptoms, because a small gland with a periurethral nodule or high smooth muscle tone can obstruct more than a large gland that expands outward.

Obstruction produces two groups of symptoms. Voiding symptoms come straight from resistance: the detrusor needs extra time and pressure to open the outlet (hesitancy), flow through a narrowed urethra is weak and interrupted, and terminal dribbling and a sense of incomplete emptying follow. Storage symptoms come from the bladder's adaptation. A detrusor working against pressure overload hypertrophies like the left ventricle in aortic stenosis, and the thickened, partly denervated muscle becomes overactive, contracting at small volumes. Combined with residual urine that reduces the space left to fill, this causes frequency, urgency, and nocturia.

blocks.title: From prostatic nodule to kidney injury
steps: Transition zone nodules and smooth muscle tone narrow the urethra
Detrusor generates higher pressure to void
Detrusor fails to empty fully: postvoid residual rises
Stasis favors infection and bladder stones
Sustained high bladder pressure dilates both ureters
Bilateral hydronephrosis; GFR falls (postrenal kidney injury)
blocks.caption: Compensation (hypertrophy) comes first and decompensation (residual urine, retention) follows; upper tract damage is a late complication of long-standing obstruction.

blocks.text: Pressure also pushes mucosa outward between the hypertrophied muscle bundles, forming small pits (cellules) and, when larger, diverticula. These are pseudodiverticula, lined by mucosa without a full muscle wall, so they cannot empty and become further sites of stasis. Residual urine is an ideal culture medium, so urinary tract infection and bladder calculi follow; the calculi form because solutes precipitate in stagnant urine.

Acute urinary retention is a sudden inability to void with a painful, palpable bladder. It occurs when an additional load tips a compensated bladder over: a drug with anticholinergic action weakens detrusor contraction, an alpha-adrenergic agonist such as a decongestant tightens the outlet, and alcohol, immobility, or infection can contribute. Chronic retention is painless; the overdistended bladder leaks small volumes, called overflow incontinence.

Upper tract damage requires obstruction severe and long enough to keep bladder pressure high. Pressure transmits up both ureters, so BPH causes bilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis, unlike a stone, which is usually unilateral. Raised tubular and Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration, so GFR falls and blood urea nitrogen and creatinine rise. Prolonged dilation compresses the parenchyma and causes tubular atrophy.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a rising creatinine to the prostate
blocks.text: A 76-year-old man has had years of weak stream and nocturia. He now has a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL (reference about 0.7 to 1.3), a palpable bladder, and a postvoid residual of 600 mL. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Work backward: two dilated kidneys with a full, palpable bladder place the block at the bladder outlet, not in the ureters. A large residual means the detrusor has decompensated. Pressure from the full bladder has risen into both collecting systems, raising Bowman's space pressure, which lowers net filtration pressure and GFR. This is postrenal kidney injury from BPH, and it is potentially reversible if the obstruction is relieved before tubular atrophy becomes permanent.

blocks.predict: Why does BPH cause bilateral hydronephrosis, while an obstructing ureteral stone usually causes hydronephrosis on one side only?
blocks.explain: BPH blocks the single outlet below the bladder, so raised bladder pressure reaches both ureters. A stone blocks one ureter above the bladder, so only that kidney is affected.

sections.title: Acute bacterial prostatitis: organisms, routes, and findings

blocks.text: Acute bacterial prostatitis is an acute suppurative infection of the gland. The prostatic ducts open into the prostatic urethra, so the commonest route is intraprostatic reflux of infected urine during voiding. Organisms can also ascend from the urethra or be introduced directly by catheterization, cystoscopy, transurethral surgery, or needle biopsy; blood-borne spread is rare. Because infected urine is the usual source, the organisms are the uropathogens that cause cystitis.

blocks.title: Causes of acute bacterial prostatitis by setting
rows: Older men, often with BPH, catheter, or recent procedure
E. coli (most common); other gram-negative rods such as Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas; less often enterococci
E. coli: gram-negative rod, lactose fermenter, fimbriae for adherence, lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin)
N. gonorrhoeae: gram-negative diplococcus. C. trachomatis: obligate intracellular, not seen on Gram stain
blocks.caption: The age split follows exposure: older men are infected from their own urinary tract, younger men from sexual contacts.

blocks.text: Older men are predisposed because BPH leaves residual urine and raises voiding pressure, which favors both bacteriuria and reflux into the ducts, and because they undergo more instrumentation. In younger men the same pathogens that cause urethritis extend into the gland, sometimes with epididymitis.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of the clinical picture
steps: Infected urine refluxes into prostatic ducts
Bacteria multiply in acini; neutrophils pour in
Edema and microabscesses swell the gland inside its capsule
Capsule stretch and inflammation cause pain and tenderness
Endotoxin and cytokines (IL-1, TNF, IL-6) cause fever and chills
Periurethral swelling causes dysuria, frequency, and possible retention
blocks.caption: Each finding traces to one step: local suppuration, capsular tension, systemic cytokines, or swelling around the urethra.

blocks.text: The onset is abrupt, with fever above 38 °C (100.4 °F), chills, and malaise, together with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and pain in the perineum, low back, or suprapubic region. Fever and rigors occur because lipopolysaccharide on gram-negative rods activates toll-like receptor 4 on macrophages, which release IL-1, TNF, and IL-6; these raise the hypothalamic set point through prostaglandin E2. The swollen gland can compress the urethra enough to cause acute retention.

On rectal examination the gland is exquisitely tender, warm, swollen, and boggy, meaning soft and edematous from fluid and pus rather than firm. Vigorous palpation can push bacteria into the bloodstream, which is why examination is gentle and massage is avoided. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria, and urine culture usually grows the organism. PSA can rise sharply because inflammation disrupts the barrier between acini and capillaries, and it falls as inflammation resolves. Microscopically, there are dense neutrophils in acini and stroma, edema, hyperemia, and in severe cases necrosis and abscesses. Complications include prostatic abscess, bacteremia and sepsis, epididymitis, and progression to chronic bacterial prostatitis.

sections.title: Acute, chronic bacterial, and chronic nonbacterial prostatitis

blocks.text: Prostatitis is sorted by time course and by whether bacteria can be found. Symptoms lasting 3 months or more are called chronic. The National Institutes of Health classification is widely used: category I is acute bacterial, category II is chronic bacterial, category III is chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome), and category IV is asymptomatic inflammation found incidentally on biopsy or in semen.

blocks.title: Three symptomatic forms of prostatitis
rows: E. coli and other gram-negative rods; gonococcus or chlamydia in young men
Same gram-negative rods, persisting in the gland
Recurrent UTIs with the same organism
3 months or more of pelvic, perineal, or ejaculatory pain
Leukocytes in some cases; no bacteria
blocks.caption: Fever separates the acute form; recurrence with one organism defines chronic bacterial; negative cultures with chronic pain define chronic nonbacterial.

blocks.text: Chronic bacterial prostatitis usually affects older men and may follow an acute episode, although many men never had one. Bacteria persist in the ducts and acini, often in biofilms on small prostatic calculi, where neutrophils cannot clear them and many antimicrobial drugs penetrate poorly across the prostatic epithelium. From this reservoir the gland reseeds the bladder from time to time, so the defining pattern is recurrent urinary tract infection with the same organism. Between episodes the infection is low grade and confined to the gland, so symptoms are limited to low back or perineal discomfort and dysuria, without fever.

Localization studies show where the bacteria live. In the four-glass (Meares-Stamey) test, the first-voided urine samples the urethra, the midstream urine samples the bladder, and expressed prostatic secretions and the urine voided after prostatic massage sample the prostate. In chronic bacterial prostatitis the prostatic samples contain far more bacteria (classically at least tenfold more) than the urethral and bladder samples. A simplified two-glass version compares urine before and after massage.

blocks.title: Worked example: one organism, three infections
blocks.text: A 62-year-old man has had three urinary tract infections in a year, each growing the same E. coli strain, with no fever between episodes and a mildly tender prostate. Recurrent infection with the identical organism means it was never eliminated, and a man without structural kidney or bladder disease most often harbors it in the prostate. Afebrile intervals exclude acute prostatitis. Positive cultures exclude chronic nonbacterial prostatitis. A culture of postmassage urine with many more bacteria than midstream urine would confirm a prostatic reservoir: chronic bacterial prostatitis.

Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis, or chronic pelvic pain syndrome, is the most common form. It is defined by at least 3 months of pain in the perineum, pelvis, penis, or testes, often with pain on ejaculation and irritative voiding symptoms, while urine and prostatic secretions grow no bacteria. An inflammatory type has leukocytes in prostatic secretions, semen, or postmassage urine; a noninflammatory type does not. The mechanism is uncertain (pelvic floor muscle dysfunction, altered pain processing, chemical irritation from urine reflux, and autoimmunity are proposed).

blocks.predict: A 40-year-old man has had 6 months of perineal pain and pain after ejaculation. Urine cultures, including postmassage urine, are repeatedly negative, but expressed prostatic secretions contain many leukocytes. Which category is this, and why is it not chronic bacterial prostatitis?
blocks.explain: Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome), inflammatory type. Leukocytes show inflammation, but chronic bacterial prostatitis requires bacteria localized to the prostate and recurrent infection with one organism.
blocks.check: The three forms table and the localization paragraph.

integration.text: Anatomy and endocrinology explain BPH. The transition zone surrounds the urethra, so a modest amount of DHT-driven hyperplasia there obstructs early, while carcinoma in the peripheral zone grows silently toward the rectum. Physiology then predicts every complication: the detrusor hypertrophies against outlet resistance as any muscle does against pressure overload, residual urine follows when it fails, and raised pressure transmitted to both kidneys lowers GFR by opposing filtration. The same obstruction links BPH to infection, because stagnant urine and high voiding pressure favor bacteriuria and reflux into prostatic ducts.

Microbiology and immunology explain prostatitis. The organism reflects the source (the man's own urinary tract in older men, sexual contacts in younger men), endotoxin-driven cytokines explain fever, and biofilm on prostatic calculi explains why chronic bacterial infection recurs with one organism. The limits are real: chronic pelvic pain syndrome has no confirmed cause, the prostate examination is often normal in chronic disease, and PSA is raised by hyperplasia and inflammation as well as by cancer, so no single finding settles the diagnosis.

summary: BPH is DHT-dependent hyperplasia of both glands and fibromuscular stroma, beginning in the transition (periurethral) zone of older men; it requires androgen and is absent in prepubertal castrates and in 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency.
Stromal 5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to DHT, which binds the androgen receptor more strongly and drives growth factor release, increased proliferation, and reduced apoptosis.

BPH glands keep their basal cell layer and the gland is smooth and rubbery; carcinoma arises mostly in the peripheral zone, loses the basal layer, and feels hard and irregular. BPH is not a precursor of carcinoma.
Outlet obstruction has a static component (nodule mass) and a dynamic component (alpha-1 adrenergic smooth muscle tone); symptoms correlate poorly with gland size.
Voiding symptoms (hesitancy, weak stream, dribbling) come from resistance; storage symptoms (frequency, urgency, nocturia) come from an overactive hypertrophied detrusor and residual urine.

Complications follow in order: detrusor hypertrophy with trabeculation and pseudodiverticula, rising residual urine, infection and stones, acute or chronic retention, and bilateral hydronephrosis with postrenal kidney injury.

Acute bacterial prostatitis comes from reflux of infected urine or instrumentation; E. coli and other gram-negative rods dominate in older men, N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis in younger sexually active men.
Acute prostatitis presents with fever, chills, dysuria, frequency, perineal pain, and an exquisitely tender, warm, boggy prostate; massage is avoided because it can cause bacteremia.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis causes recurrent urinary infections with the same organism from a prostatic reservoir, often biofilm on calculi, shown by localization cultures.
Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome) is the most common form: 3 months or more of pelvic pain with no bacteria and no fever.

verify: Age-related prevalence of histologic BPH (commonly quoted as about 20% at age 40, about 70% at 60, and about 90% at 80) varies between sources; the chapter says only that it is present in most men by their 80s.
The proportion of carcinomas arising in the peripheral zone is quoted at about 70% to 75% and the transition zone share differs among series; confirm whether NABNE expects a number.
The role of estrogen in BPH and the specific growth factors involved (FGF7 and other FGF family members, TGF-beta) are supported but not settled; the chapter states them cautiously.
The role of C. trachomatis in acute and chronic prostatitis is debated in the urologic literature even though board resources list it with N. gonorrhoeae for younger men; confirm NABNE's position.

The relative frequency of the prostatitis categories differs between sources; all agree chronic nonbacterial is by far the most common, but whether acute or chronic bacterial is rarer is not consistent, so the chapter calls both uncommon.

The leukocyte threshold for an inflammatory specimen of expressed prostatic secretions (often more than 10 leukocytes per high-power field) and the tenfold bacterial gradient in the four-glass test come from urologic sources; confirm whether NABNE tests exact values.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponym Meares-Stamey and the NIH category numbers or only the descriptive names.
